added_claim_errors: '$2,400 becomes $1,751 (in 2027 dollars)': this silently adds the 3.6% COLA (1,690 x 1.036). The key gives about $1,690, and the December 2026 COLA does not apply to someone first eligible in 2027 (my own knowledge). This is the key's COLA side-claim trap.

'First check lands in May, so only nine payments fall in the year': May to December is eight payments. With whole-check withholding of the April to July benefits, almost nothing arrives until about September (key).

'Actual 2027 total is $47,538' and 'net about $9,500 in benefits': this overstates 2027 cash. It spreads the $6,220 across nine checks instead of withholding whole checks; about four deposits (about $7,000) actually arrive.

'Roughly $134/month extra federal in 2027, $168/month at full-year rates': these are computed on gross benefits before the earnings-test withholding, and withheld benefits are not taxable income. Overstated and unverifiable.
The 12-month 'Monthly average' table (SS net $1,232.51, total $4,399.17 a month, $52,790 a year) contradicts its own nine-payment statement and is misleading.

'Roughly $1,170/month less': this compares against the 12-payment $4,399 figure, not the stated actual 2027 average of $3,961 (which would be about $1,606 less). The arithmetic is internally inconsistent.
'I put a full one-pager in social-security-2027-budget.md': it refers to a file the person does not have, so this cannot be verified.
'First week of entitlement is April': there is no 'first week' concept. Entitlement is monthly.
'Give up about $735/month for life': this rests on COLA-inflated figures (2,486 - 1,751).

'Claiming at 62 is 60 months early... equals a 30% reduction': this contradicts its own later statement that entitlement starts April 2027, which means 59 months and 29.58% (key). The approximation is acceptable but inconsistent.

'x 1.036 (2027 COLA) = about $1,740 in 2027 dollars': this adds the 3.6% COLA as certain. That COLA does not apply to someone first eligible in 2027, and the key gives about $1,690. This is the key's side-claim trap.
'If you waited until you stopped working, or until 67, you'd lock in roughly $2,486 a month': stopping work before 67 would still leave a reduced benefit. The $2,486 figure is also COLA-inflated.

'Your first payment would arrive in May': under the earnings test the April to July checks are withheld, so the first deposit comes about September. Its own 'four actual deposits' line partly corrects this.

The SSA 2027 COLA fact sheet link returned 403 when I opened it. The figures it cites ($25,560 for 2027, $24,480 for 2026) match the key. I opened the POMS RS 00615.015 link and it confirms the 'age 62 throughout the entire month' rule.

reasons: Both answers correct both premises at the start. Both get the earnings test right ($25,560 limit, $12,440 excess, $6,220 withheld), and both fall into the COLA trap ($1,751 and $1,740 instead of about $1,690). A has the more precise reduction (April, 59 months, 29.58%). But its 2027 budget is wrong: it says the first check comes in May and that nine payments arrive in 2027, it never mentions whole-check withholding, and it computes tax on gross benefits. Together these overstate 2027 benefit cash by about $2,500. B explains whole-check withholding and correctly expects about four deposits (about $7,000) in 2027. Its full-year federal tax estimate checks out, and it handles Medicare correctly. Its errors are smaller: a 60-month figure that contradicts its own April start, and a confusing 'first payment in May' line. Neither answer suggests checking with my Social Security or SSA's calculators.
